title: Why didn’t Heloise rebel in Portrait of a Lady on Fire?

commenti.body:
Yes, it’s a little ridiculous that their love is put up on this platform and then they accept so quickly that it can’t happen. They’re in a better position than most people at that time to carry on a relationship. 

Heloise was marrying a rich guy and could have hired Marianne in some capacity. Or Marianne could have provided for them since she actually had a job where so could make money. It might not have led to an easy life, but they don’t even seem to contemplate it.

It’s very weird to me to make a movie about artists/artistically inclined people where they aren’t pushing the boundaries of what can be done at the time.

I loved this movie. Thank you for making me think of it.

All I can say is that we are so far removed from the period of time portrayed that it might be hard to appreciate the difficulties of the choice. 

Hell, TODAY, in the West, there are people living a lie because of their fears about coming out with their identity and they aren't even concerned that someone is going to cut their head off.

That concert scene though... Damn. I remember having to catch my breath it was so powerful.

Gender inequality and gender roles are integral to the story of POALOF. 

If this film was set in modern times, then they may have eloped and ended up happily ever after. But the point is that women, especially Heloise, have a role to fulfil in society (wife/mother), no matter her preference of lifestyle/career, lover, or even sexuality.

This is likely what the significance of Heloise and Marianne helping Sophie to get an abortion is about — they don't want her life, individuality and 'freedom' to be cut short and for her to have to play her role as a woman/mother for the rest of her life.

I hate it when modern audiences apply contemporary values to historical time periods. It’s pretty obvious why she would make that choice, the historicity of heteronormativity is integral to the plot and conflict of the film. 

You’re being obtuse and this post is unnecessary.

The rest of the posts here address the rest of the question but I think your idea about her not seeing her isn't necessarily correct. 

The film is ambiguous about whether or not she is aware of her presence but I think the combination of the work being the piece they bonded over which would lead to an argument that she, especially as she is alone, has gone to the performance of this piece in the hopes that she will be there, and therefore is looking for her.

As well, the fact that in not making direct eye contact she reaffirms the choice she made to accept societal expectations but also signals through her emotion that she still loves her but cannot bring herself to acknowledge it any further even with a glance. Incredibly powerful and heartbreaking.
How has your movie watching gone?
